content:
# Deuteronomy 6 — Disagreement Log
**Chapter:** Deuteronomy 6 (25 verses)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA
**Total disagreements logged:** 22

---

## V.1 — "ordinances" vs. "judgments"

- **EMET:** "the statutes and the ordinances"
- **LOGOS:** "the statutes and the judgments"
- **PNEUMA:** "the statutes and the ordinances"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the statutes and the ordinances" (EMET/PNEUMA). Per established convention: *mishpatim* in Deuteronomic legal context = "ordinances." LOGOS's "judgments" implies a narrower judicial sense.

---

## V.1 — Framing of the opening sentence

- **EMET:** "And this [is] the commandment, the statutes and the ordinances that the LORD your God commanded to teach you to do..."
- **LOGOS:** "Now this is the commandment — the statutes and the judgments — that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you..."
- **PNEUMA:** "Now this is the commandment — the statutes and the ordinances — that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you..."
- **SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS/PNEUMA framing ("Now this is the commandment...") adopted. The Hebrew *ve-zot ha-mitzvah* opens with an emphatic *ve* (and/now). LOGOS adds "me" (the implied object of *le-lammedkha*) explicitly — SOPHIA retains this as it clarifies Moses as speaker.

---

## V.3 — "Hear therefore" vs. "And you shall hear"

- **EMET:** "And you shall hear, O Yisra'el, and you shall take heed to do [it]"
- **LOGOS:** "Hear therefore, O Israel, and take care to do them"
- **PNEUMA:** "Hear, O Israel, and be careful to follow them"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Hear therefore, O Israel, and take care to do them" (LOGOS). The connective "therefore" links v.3 to the purpose clauses of vv.1–2 and anticipates the Shema of v.4. PNEUMA's "follow" for *la'asotam* is interpretively weaker than "do."

---

## V.4 — echad: "one" vs. "alone" (THE SHEMA)

- **EMET:** "the LORD our God, the LORD [is] one"
- **LOGOS:** "the LORD our God, the LORD is one"
- **PNEUMA:** "The LORD is our God. The LORD alone."
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the LORD our God, the LORD is one" (EMET/LOGOS). This is the most consequential ruling in this chapter. The Hebrew *echad* is the cardinal number "one." PNEUMA's "alone" (*levado* in Hebrew) is a theologically defensible reading in context but lacks textual support in ancient witnesses: the LXX Vaticanus (p. 148) reads *Κύριος εἷς ἐστιν* — "the LORD is one" — using *heis* (one), not *monos* (alone). Mark 12:29 cites the same. PNEUMA also restructures the verse into two sentences ("The LORD is our God. The LORD alone.") which breaks the traditional four-word Hebrew formula. SOPHIA preserves the unified structure and "one."

---

## V.5 — nafshekha: "soul" vs. "being"

- **EMET:** "with all your soul"
- **LOGOS:** "with all your soul"
- **PNEUMA:** "with all your being"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "with all your soul" (EMET/LOGOS). Per DEU 004 v.29 ruling: *nefesh* in Shema-language = "soul" for consistency throughout Deuteronomy.

---

## V.5 — me'odekha: "might" vs. "strength"

- **EMET:** "with all your might"
- **LOGOS:** "with all your might"
- **PNEUMA:** "with all your strength"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "with all your strength" (PNEUMA). Both are accurate for the unusual substantive *me'od*. "Strength" flows more naturally in the English triad with "heart" and "soul."

---

## V.5 — ve-ahavta: "And you shall love" vs. "Love"

- **EMET:** "And you shall love the LORD your God"
- **LOGOS:** "And you shall love the LORD your God"
- **PNEUMA:** "Love the LORD your God"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "And you shall love the LORD your God" (EMET/LOGOS). The Hebrew *ve-ahavta* is a waw-consecutive perfect with imperatival force — the conjunction "And" is part of the clause structure and connects v.5 to v.4. PNEUMA's bare imperative ("Love") is natural but loses the structural connection.

---

## V.6 — "upon your heart" vs. "on your heart"

- **EMET:** "shall be upon your heart"
- **LOGOS:** "shall be on your heart"
- **PNEUMA:** "are to be on your heart"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "shall be on your heart" (LOGOS). The Hebrew *al-levavekha* = "upon/on your heart." SOPHIA notes that EMET's "upon" is slightly more literal and preserves the spatial image (the word resting *upon* the heart, not yet *in* it — as the LXX harmonizes with *en*). However "on" (LOGOS) is equally valid and more natural. PNEUMA's "are to be" introduces a modal construction not in the Hebrew.

---

## V.7 — shinnantam: "teach diligently" vs. "repeat sharply" vs. "recite"

- **EMET:** "you shall repeat them sharply to your sons"
- **LOGOS:** "you shall teach them diligently to your children"
- **PNEUMA:** "Recite them to your children"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "you shall teach them diligently to your children" (LOGOS). The Pi'el of *shanan* (to sharpen/incise) connotes drilling through repetition until the teaching cuts deep. EMET's "repeat them sharply" is technically precise but awkward. PNEUMA's "recite" loses the pedagogical force — recitation can be passive; the Hebrew implies active deep-drilling. LOGOS's "diligently" captures the intensity.

---

## V.7 — "sons" vs. "children"

- **EMET:** "to your sons"
- **LOGOS:** "to your children"
- **PNEUMA:** "to your children"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "to your children" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). The Hebrew *le-vanekha* is literally "to your sons" (*banim*) — but the catechetical context implies all offspring. The gendered translation (EMET) is technically correct but the inclusive rendering is functionally appropriate here.

---

## V.8 — totafot: transliteration and gloss

- **EMET:** "as frontlets [totafot] between your eyes"
- **LOGOS:** "as frontlets between your eyes"
- **PNEUMA:** "a symbol on your forehead"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "as frontlets [totafot] between your eyes" (EMET). PNEUMA's "symbol on your forehead" renders the practice rather than the term — it removes the hapax *totafot* entirely. Project convention preserves technical/obscure terms with a bracketed gloss. LOGOS drops the transliteration; SOPHIA restores it.

---

## V.9 — mezuzot: transliteration

- **EMET:** "upon the doorposts [mezuzot] of your house"
- **LOGOS:** "on the doorposts of your house"
- **PNEUMA:** "on the doorposts of your house"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "on the doorposts [mezuzot] of your house" (EMET, adapted). *Mezuzah* later gave its name to a specific practice; the transliteration with gloss is preserved per project convention. "On" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) preferred over "upon" (EMET) for naturalness.

---

## V.12 — "house of slaves" vs. "house of slavery"

- **EMET:** "from the house of slaves"
- **LOGOS:** "out of the house of slavery"
- **PNEUMA:** "out of the place of slavery"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "out of the house of slaves" (EMET, preposition adapted). Hebrew *beit avadim* = "house of slaves" — the concrete noun *avadim* (slaves/servants). "House of slavery" (LOGOS) abstracts the term; "place of slavery" (PNEUMA) further abstracts and changes the architectural image. The concreteness of "slaves" is theologically pointed — this is a house full of enslaved persons, not merely an institution.

---

## V.13 — word order (inverted emphasis)

- **EMET:** "The LORD your God you shall fear, and him you shall serve, and by his name you shall swear"
- **LOGOS:** "You shall fear the LORD your God, and him you shall serve, and by his name you shall swear"
- **PNEUMA:** "Fear the LORD your God, serve him, and swear by his name alone"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "The LORD your God you shall fear, and him you shall serve, and by his name you shall swear" (EMET). The Hebrew fronts the object — "YHWH Elohekha tira'" — placing the divine name first for rhetorical emphasis. This emphasis is integral to the prohibition context (vv.14–15). PNEUMA adds "alone" at the end — this is not in the MT.

---

## V.16 — "put to the test" vs. "test"

- **EMET:** "You shall not test the LORD your God"
- **LOGOS:** "You shall not put the LORD your God to the test"
- **PNEUMA:** "Do not put the LORD your God to the test"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "You shall not put the LORD your God to the test" (LOGOS). The fuller formulation "put...to the test" reflects the weight of the Hebrew *nasah* in context and avoids the ambiguity of bare "test." PNEUMA's imperative form is less literal than the *lo* + imperfect prohibition construction in the Hebrew.

---

## V.18 — "in the sight of" vs. "in the eyes of"

- **EMET:** "the right and the good in the eyes of the LORD"
- **LOGOS:** "what is right and good in the sight of the LORD"
- **PNEUMA:** "what is right and good in the LORD's sight"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "what is right and good in the sight of the LORD" (LOGOS). Hebrew *be-einei YHWH* = "in the eyes of the LORD." EMET's "the right and the good" with the definite article is literal and preserves the Deuteronomic formula (*ha-yashar ve-ha-tov*); SOPHIA retains "what is right and good" for naturalness while keeping the idiom.

---

## V.20 — "ordinances" vs. "judgments" (second occurrence)

- **EMET:** "the testimonies and the statutes and the ordinances"
- **LOGOS:** "the testimonies and the statutes and the judgments"
- **PNEUMA:** "these testimonies, statutes, and ordinances"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the testimonies and the statutes and the ordinances" (EMET/PNEUMA). Consistent with the ruling at v.1.

---

## V.21 — "strong hand" vs. "mighty hand"

- **EMET:** "with a strong hand"
- **LOGOS:** "with a mighty hand"
- **PNEUMA:** "with a mighty hand"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "with a strong hand" (EMET). Hebrew *yad chazaqah* — *chazaq* = strong/firm. Per project convention established at DEU 004 v.34: "strong hand" for *yad chazaqah* throughout. LOGOS/PNEUMA's "mighty" (*gibbor* or *gadol*) is a different Hebrew root.

---

## V.22 — ra'im: "evil" vs. "calamitous" vs. "devastating"

- **EMET:** "great and evil — against Mitsrayim"
- **LOGOS:** "great and calamitous, against Egypt"
- **PNEUMA:** "great and devastating signs and wonders"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "great and calamitous signs and wonders against Egypt" (LOGOS). Hebrew *ra'im* = evil/terrible/harmful. "Evil" (EMET) is accurate but could be misread morally; "calamitous" (LOGOS) and "devastating" (PNEUMA) both convey the destructive character from the Egyptian perspective. "Calamitous" (LOGOS) is slightly more precise for *ra'im* in this context. SOPHIA also adopts LOGOS's word order: "great and calamitous signs and wonders" (adjectives before noun rather than EMET's parenthetical dash structure).

---

## V.23 — "us he brought out" vs. "he brought us out" (word order)

- **EMET:** "And us he brought out from there in order to bring us in"
- **LOGOS:** "And he brought us out from there, so that he might bring us in"
- **PNEUMA:** "And he brought us out from there to bring us in"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "And us he brought out from there in order to bring us in" (EMET). The Hebrew *ve-otanu* fronts the pronoun — "and us he brought out" — as a rhetorical contrast with the fathers who received the oath (v.23b). The emphasis on "us" as the direct recipients of the exodus is part of the catechetical force of this passage (cf. Passover haggadah: "not our ancestors alone, but us"). LOGOS/PNEUMA normalize and lose this emphasis.

---

## V.24 — "for our good all the days" vs. "for our lasting good"

- **EMET:** "for our good all the days"
- **LOGOS:** "for our lasting good"
- **PNEUMA:** "for our own good always"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "for our lasting good" (LOGOS). Hebrew *le-tovah lanu kol ha-yamim* = "for good to us all the days." LOGOS's "lasting good" is a clean compression that preserves the permanence. EMET is more literal; PNEUMA's "our own good" adds a reflexive emphasis not in the MT.

---

## V.25 — "when we take heed" vs. "if we take care"

- **EMET:** "when we take heed to do all this commandment"
- **LOGOS:** "if we take care to do all this commandment"
- **PNEUMA:** "to be careful to follow all this commandment"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "when we take care to do all this commandment" (EMET/LOGOS, combined). Hebrew *ki nishmor* — the particle *ki* here functions as "when/if." EMET's "when" presents obedience as anticipated rather than conditional; LOGOS's "if" introduces conditionality. In context, following the catechetical declaration, "when" is preferable — this is a statement of communal intent. "Take care" (LOGOS) is preferred over "take heed" (EMET) for naturalness.
